messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary for Case 1:

Patient Information:
Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 40 years
Gender: Male

Admission Information:
The patient was admitted to the hospital on [REDACTED] with symptoms of general malaise, arthralgia in his extremities, facial cyanosis, and fever (39°C). A medical history of post-traumatic splenectomy was reported.

Hospital Course:
Upon admission, empirical antibiotic therapy was started with ceftriaxone and vancomycin as the patient was diagnosed with secondary sepsis caused by meningitis from Streptococcus pneumoniae. Due to a severe hemodynamic instability, the patient was transferred to the ICU where they exhibited persistent hypotension and an inflammatory state with high levels of CRP and PCT.

The patient underwent continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) in hemodiafiltration mode for a total of 68 hours along with Cytosorb cartridge. During this treatment, a general improvement was observed in terms of the patient's hemodynamic and metabolic stability as well as reducing levels of PCT and CRP. The patient's norepinephrine demand decreased significantly throughout the treatment and the patient could be stopped from CRRT after 12 days.

Discharge Information:
After further treatment and observation, the patient was discharged on [REDACTED]. At the time of discharge, the patient was alert, collaborative, tracheotomized, and spontaneously breathing with a recovery of diuresis. The patient was advised to continue with follow-up appointments according to the recommended medical protocols.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Recommendations:
The patient was advised to follow up with medical appointments as per recommended medical protocols.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
Overwhelming pneumococcal sepsis with septic shock, in an asplenic patient and secondary to meningitis, was chiefly responsible for this admission and the ICU care. Under Australian Coding Standards, sepsis present on admission is sequenced ahead of its localised source (pneumococcal meningitis, G00.1). Pneumococcal sepsis is in chapter A, category A40 (streptococcal sepsis).

CODE: A40
